449: Bid protest merits: whether the Contracting Officer incorrectly rejected the unsolicited proposal as not valid under FAR 15.603(c) and 15.606-1; not reached on merits because standing failed
Mr. Diaz has failed to demonstrate that the Contracting Officer incorrectly determined that his proposal was not "valid"
789: Bid protest merits: the 2014 RFQ payment terms violate FAR Part 12's prohibition on terms inconsistent with customary commercial practice, so the protest is sustained.

the revised payment terms violate FAR Part 12's prohibition against including contract terms inconsistent with customary commercial practice, we reverse the Court of Federal Claims grant of judgment on the administrative record to the government.
2228: Bid protest merits: whether the Air Force's decision to reopen the bidding based on disparate IR&D communications was rational and whether the intervenor was prejudiced; the protest was denied.
We affirm, concluding that the reopening decision was proper based on the disparate-information violation.
2387: Bid protest merits: contracting officer's non-responsibility determination and referral to the SBA was not arbitrary or capricious; protest denied.

The Court of Federal Claims correctly concluded that the contracting officer had a reasonable basis for the determination of non-responsibility and that the SBA had a reasonable basis to deny her a COC.
2388: Bid protest merits: SBA's denial of a Certificate of Competency was not arbitrary or capricious and the SBA did not exceed its authority; protest denied.
We also conclude that the SBA had a reasonable basis to deny Ms. Sims a COC.
2401: Bid protest merits: whether SBA-OHA's determination that the primary and vital requirements were a coordinated package of lodging and transportation services lacked a rational basis; protest denied
In short, Tinton Falls fails to meet its high burden of showing that the SBA-OHA's determination lacked a rational basis.
2746: Bid protest merits: whether the GPO was required to refer the non-responsibility determination to the SBA under 15 U.S.C. § 637(b)(7) (statutory scope of 'Government procurement officer' and 'Government contract'); court held no referral required, protest denied
we decide that the GPO is not required to refer such determinations to the SBA
2747: Bid protest merits: whether the GPO's non-responsibility determination and award lacked a rational basis or violated procurement regulations with prejudice; court held the award was not arbitrary or capricious
The GPO provided a coherent and reasonable explanation of its exercise of discretion in the D&F itself.
3277: Bid protest merits: agency authority to take corrective action and re-evaluate proposals, and whether Guardian's flood plain report satisfied the solicitation; Claims Court denial of Guardian's motion for judgment on the administrative record affirmed.
The Claims Court did not clearly err in finding that Guardian's flood plain report did not satisfy the relevant provision of the solicitation
4022: Bid protest merits: whether State's refusal to disqualify AAR for obtaining and using allegedly proprietary DynCorp information (salary data and profit margin analysis) was arbitrary or unlawful; the court held the contracting officer's responsibility determination had a rational basis and denied the protest on this ground.
Under such circumstances, the contracting officer had a rational basis for his decision not to disqualify AAR based upon its receipt of the stale DynCorp salary information referenced by Hamilton.
4024: Bid protest merits: alleged unequal treatment because AAR's proposal also contemplated transferring MIS maintenance to the IT Associate Contractor; the court held State rationally read AAR's proposal and denied the protest on this ground.

DynCorp contends that State should have disqualified AAR because AAR, like DynCorp, proposed that the IT Associate Contractor would be responsible for MIS operations and maintenance following transition from the AWIS. This argument fails.
4025: Bid protest merits: whether the agency properly considered AAR's cross-referenced response to a discussion notice (TEN 010) in evaluating its staffing proposal; the court held the agency did not err and denied the protest on this ground.
State did not err when it considered AAR's response to TEN 010, see J.A. 112759–66, when evaluating its staffing proposal.
4480: Bid protest merits: the contracting officer's rejection of SBSI's nonconforming proposal for failure to redact was reasonable and not arbitrary; protest denied.
The CO's decision to reject the nonconforming proposal in these circumstances was reasonable and well within the CO's discretion.
4527: Bid protest merits: whether the Army's J&A justifying sole-source award of sixteen UH-72A helicopters to Airbus was arbitrary and capricious and lacked a rational basis.

We conclude, however, that the agency provided a coherent and reasonable explanation of its exercise of discretion, and therefore the justifications for the sole-source award are not arbitrary and capricious.
4548: Single-source award under 10 U.S.C. 2304a(d)(3): Claims Court's finding that the Under Secretary's chosen exception did not fit the contract was affirmed as a legal error favoring the protester
The Claims Court properly rejected the government's argument.
4549: Prejudice from the single-source legal error: no prejudice found because Oracle would not have had a substantial chance of award even under multiple awards
is not clearly erroneous. We therefore will not disturb the Claims Court's determination that the case did not need to be remanded
4550: Gate 1.2 as a 'qualification requirement' under 10 U.S.C. 2319: Gate 1.2 held not a qualification requirement
The Claims Court correctly held that Gate 1.2 does not constitute a 'qualification requirement' within the meaning of section 2319.
4551: Competitive procedures under 10 U.S.C. 2304 and FAR 6.302-1: Gate 1.2 did not convert the procurement into one using other than full and open competition
we agree with the Claims Court that the FedRAMP Moderate authorization component of Gate 1.2 did not transform the solicitation into one for less than full and open competition.
4552: Reasonableness of Gate 1.2 and whether the solicitation unduly restricted competition: Oracle did not show the security need was unreasonable
Oracle has not shown that the Department's determination as to its need for a level of security represented by Gate 1.2 was unreasonable
4553: Organizational and individual conflicts of interest: contracting officer's no-effect determination upheld, and the solicitation need not be set aside
we agree with the Claims Court that the conflict of interest problems of those three individuals had no effect on the JEDI Cloud solicitation.
5123: Bid protest merits: whether the Army's corrective action (reopening the procurement) was arbitrary or lacked a rational basis; the court held the CFC applied an incorrect 'narrowly targeted' standard and that the corrective action was rationally related to the procurement defects.

Accordingly, we hold that the original corrective action was rationally related to the procurement defect and that the Court of Federal Claims abused its discretion in finding that Appellees demonstrated, inter alia, success on the merits.
5404: Bid protest merits: VA's price/cost-savings evaluation methodology (absolute vs. relative savings) was rational and the protest on this ground was denied
The VA did not act irrationally by choosing one of two equivalent methodologies.
5405: Bid protest merits: unequal treatment claim under the Corporate Experience/Capability subfactor; protest denied for lack of demonstrated prejudice
Since WellPoint has not shown prejudice, there is no basis for setting aside the award based on the alleged unequal treatment.
5706: Bid protest merits: whether the VA contracting officer's decision to cancel the roof replacement solicitation lacked a rational basis and was arbitrary or capricious; the protest was denied.
In sum, we find that the contracting officer had a rational basis to cancel the roof replacement solicitation.
5805: Bid protest merits: whether CBP's determination that ISS's collective experience supported a High Confidence rating and phase-two advancement was arbitrary, capricious, or contrary to law; protest denied.

On this record, we hold that the Court of Federal Claims did not err in holding that CBP's determination that ISS's experience and risk awareness/mitigation supported a "High Confidence" rating was not arbitrary, capricious, or in violation of law.
5966: Bid protest challenge that the VA's reliance on Attachment 15 to evaluate technical proposals was inconsistent with the RFP; court held the VA gave clear, reasonable notice and denied the protest.
Thus, contrary to ODG's contention, the record establishes that the VA provided clear, reasonable notice that the VA planned to use Attachment 15 to evaluate proposals.
5967: Bid protest challenge that the VA disparately evaluated ODG's technical proposal compared with awardees; court found most disparate-treatment claims failed on substantive differences and that the two proven instances were not prejudicial, so the protest was denied.
ODG cannot prevail on most of its claims of disparate treatment.
5993: Bid protest merits: whether the SBA's determination that XOtech was ineligible for SDVO set-aside contracts (under 13 C.F.R. § 125.13(d), requiring SDV control of all decisions) was arbitrary or otherwise unlawful; the court held the determination lawful and denied XOtech's challenge.
We agree with the government and the Claims Court that XOtech is not an SDVO business.
6068: Bid protest merits: whether the Army's pre-award market research and commercial-item determination under 10 U.S.C. § 2377 was arbitrary, capricious, or contrary to law, and the protest was sustained.

On this record, we agree with the trial court that the Army failed in its obligation under § 2377 to determine whether a commercial item could meet or be modified to meet the Army's procurement requirements.
6855: Bid protest merits: whether the VA was required under the VBA's Rule of Two (38 U.S.C. § 8127(d)) to perform a restricted-competition analysis before procuring eyewear from the Industries for the Blind under the JWOD/AbilityOne List, so the protest was sustained and the injunction affirmed.

Thus, where a product or service is on the List and ordinarily would result in the contract being awarded to a nonprofit qualified under the JWOD, the VBA unambiguously demands that priority be given to veteran-owned small businesses.
7105: Bid protest merits: court upheld DISA's cost realism review of Agile's within-deviation labor rates and denied the protest as not arbitrary or contrary to the solicitation.
7133: Bid protest merits: whether CBP's failure to consult with the SBA was a significant, prejudicial error; the court held ARC did not show prejudice and the protest was denied.

we find that even if CBP needed to consult with the SBA under 13 C.F.R. § 125.2(c)(2), which we do not decide here, ARC fails to show that CBP's failure to do so affected the outcome of its decision to issue the 2018 RFQ unrestricted.
7281: Bid protest merits on Counts III and IV: whether GSA's choice of the $26.00 PSF maximum rental rate was arbitrary, capricious, or lacking a rational basis; judgment on the administrative record for the government was affirmed.
Under our highly deferential standard of review, we affirm the Claims Court's grant of judgment on the administrative record with respect to Counts III and IV.
7367: Bid protest merits: the Award Limitations Policy in the Jurisdiction H solicitation precluded full and open competition under CICA and the FAR, so the protest is sustained.
Because we hold that the JH solicitation did not provide for full and open competition, we then address whether the agency's approach was otherwise permissible.
7368: Bid protest merits: the government's argument that the workload caps were 'procurement procedures otherwise expressly authorized by statute' under 41 U.S.C. § 3301(a) (via 42 U.S.C. § 1395kk-1) was rejected, so the protest is sustained.
We therefore reject the government's argument that the workload caps are 'procurement procedures otherwise expressly authorized by statute' under § 3301(a).
7890: Bid protest merits: the court held that M.R. Pittman waived its protest grounds under the Blue & Gold waiver rule because the omitted NAICS code was a patent defect it failed to raise before the close of bidding, so the protest was denied.
In sum, we agree with the trial court that M.R. Pittman waived its protest grounds under the Blue & Gold waiver rule.
8595: Bid protest merits: whether the cancellation of the '181 solicitation lacked a rational basis or violated regulation or procedure; the protest was denied.
we see no "lack[] [of] a rational basis" or "violation of regulation or procedure" in the cancellation decision.
8596: Bid protest merits: whether the '276 solicitation should have been set aside for SDVOSBs under the Rule of Two; the protest was denied because the twin expectations were not met.
Because the twin expectations of the Rule of Two were not met, there was no requirement to set aside the '276 solicitation for competition among veteran-owned businesses.
8714: Bid protest merits: protester argued the Army violated FAR 15.404-1 by bypassing the preferred price-analysis techniques without the required predicate determinations; court held the FAR provisions are permissive and the protest was denied.
FAR 15.404-1(b)(3) does not conditionally prohibit a contracting officer from using any particular price-analysis technique.
8715: Bid protest merits: protester argued the Army's price-reasonableness conclusion was arbitrary and capricious for failing to account for price disparities among offers; court found no arbitrary or capricious action and denied the protest.
There was therefore no problematic aspect of the price disparity to address, and therefore no important aspect of the problem left unconsidered.
8891: Bid protest merits: whether the Army reasonably assigned CACI a technical deficiency for omitting dongle size measurements and whether disparate treatment occurred; court held the deficiency was reasonable and the protest denied.
The Claims Court did not err in sustaining the contracting officer's finding of a technical deficiency.
9056: Bid protest merits: whether the VA's competitive range and evaluation of rival bids were challenged; the court did not reach the merits and remanded for merits consideration, so no merits ruling was made

We reverse this portion of the judgment and remand for the Court of Federal Claims to address the merits of REV's claims attacking the VA's assessment of competing bids and its establishment of the competitive range.
9070: Bid protest merits: whether the VA's award to a non-SDVOSB contractor under the Rule of Two and tiered precedence had a rational basis and no regulatory violation; protest denied

Because the procurement officer's decision to award the solicitation to a contractor other than Land Shark had a rational basis and was not a violation of regulation or procedure, we affirm the Court of Federal Claims' decision.
9247: Bid protest merits: whether the agency's irrational assignment of a strength to CAE's proposal was prejudicial enough to set aside the award; court held protester must show prejudice and found no prejudice.
We see no departure from the correct legal standard in the Claims Court's prejudice analysis.
9248: Presumption of prejudice when agency decision is irrational: court rejected presumption and held protester must show prejudice under the usual standard.
We hold that there is no presumption of prejudice when a protestor demonstrates irrationality in an agency decision.
9368: Bid protest merits: challenge that the Army improperly failed to terminate KOVR's award under the SBA small business regulation, rejected because the RSA priority controls.
We agree that the Army's treatment of the RSA as trumping the small business provision was not unlawful
9369: Bid protest merits: challenge that KOVR's proposal violated the DOD-DOE Joint Statement of Policy requiring a blind manager per military dining facility; rejected because the RSA controls and the Joint Statement has no binding effect.

We thus agree with the Claims Court that there is no legal requirement that blind persons had to be engaged at all service locations, and that it was not “contrary to law” for the Army to select KOVR’s RSA proposal for the solicitation.
9370: Bid protest merits: alleged Procurement Integrity Act violation based on use of incumbent-contract performance information; rejected because it is not contractor bid or proposal information.
We thus conclude that Mitchco has not established a PIA violation.
9371: Bid protest merits: challenge to the Army's technical and responsibility evaluation of KOVR's proposal, including Southern's alleged unwillingness to perform and the lack of a signed subcontract; rejected as lacking hard facts.
There is thus no merit to these claims, and we will not delve any further into the “minutiae of the procurement process” by second guessing the agency’s evaluation of KOVR’s proposal.
9487: Bid protest merits: agency's evaluation of protester's proposed price and of subfactor three and six strengths was not arbitrary, capricious, or unlawful; protest denied.
On this record, we hold that the Court of Federal Claims did not err in holding that the agency's evaluation of Red Cedar's proposed price was not arbitrary, capricious, or in violation of law.
9978: Bid protest merits: timeliness of awardee's proposal after the one-day deadline extension; court held the contracting officer reasonably extended the deadline before it expired, so the protest was denied
We find no error in the Claims Court's determination that the Army Corps properly extended the proposal deadline by one day.
9979: Bid protest merits: reasonableness of past performance evaluation, including relevance ratings, unequal treatment, and joint venture experience; court found no error and protest denied
We decline to second-guess or otherwise disturb the SSA's reasonable and discretionary relevance determination.
10190: Bid protest merits: the Government's elimination of Safeguard's proposal was not arbitrary; the solicitation gave notice that exceptions to the line item structure could lead to elimination, the omissions were material and could not be cured by clarification or waiver, and protest denied.

The Claims Court similarly did not err by determining that Safeguard's omissions of the pricing information for CLINs X007AA and X007AB were material, not resolvable by clarifications, nor subject to waiver.
10548: Bid protest merits: the contracting officer's price reasonableness analysis was not shown to be improper, so the protest on that ground fails.

This argument is unavailing because the VA website is not a regulation that the contracting officer was required to follow and because the discussion that Land Shark refers to concerned FAR Part 15, not FAR 13.106-3.
10739: Bid protest merits: court held the printing mandate (44 U.S.C. § 501), as narrowly construed under constitutional avoidance, does not apply to the solicitation, reversing the judgment denying the protest.
we reverse the Court of Federal Claims' determination that the printing mandate applied to the solicitation at issue here
11018: Bid protest merits: whether State's cancellation and resolicitation decision lacked a rational basis and was arbitrary and capricious under the APA.
We conclude that State's decision to cancel and resolicit the contract (which included Torres as a prospective bidder) lacks a rational basis.
11019: Bid protest merits: whether the contracting officer's disclosure of SAGAM's proposal information violated the Procurement Integrity Act, affirmed as a merits finding underlying the protest.
We agree with the Claims Court that the contracting officer's disclosure of information taken from SAGAM's proposal constitutes a PIA violation that impacted the procurement.
11036: Bid protest merits of Count I: challenge to the agency's technical evaluation and assignment of risks to Harmonia's proposal; protest denied.

Harmonia fails to establish that the Bureau acted arbitrarily, capriciously, or contrary to the terms of the solicitation when it determined that while Harmonia's proposed cross-training of staff and peer-testing of code had certain potential advantages, they also had potential disadvantages.
11037: Bid protest merits of Count III: challenge to the agency's best-value tradeoff determination selecting Alethix; protest denied.
Harmonia likewise fails to show that the Bureau erred in concluding that Alethix's proposal represented the best value for the agency.
11111: Bid protest merits: whether the SBA's size determination that Obsidian was not a small business was arbitrary or capricious, given the claim that the Runway Extension Act required a five-year averaging period. The court held the REA did not apply to the SBA, so the protest fails.

Having agreed with the Court of Federal Claims that the SBA's size determination was not arbitrary or capricious because the REA did not apply to the SBA, we also hold that the court did not abuse its discretion in denying injunctive relief.
11233: Bid protest merits: whether the Navy contracting officer's determination that the PBL solicitation did not violate the bundling regulation was arbitrary or unlawful; protest denied.
The Navy CO did not err in determining that the bundling regulation was not violated.
11933: Bid protest merits: Army Corps determination that Anders's proposal lacked the required lost-diver plan was not arbitrary or capricious; Claims Court error reversed, protest denied
It was not arbitrary and capricious for the Army Corps contracting officer to find that Anders's proposal lacked the required lost-diver plan.
11934: Bid protest merits: Army Corps determination that Anders's outline of administrative and record-keeping procedures was inadequate was not arbitrary or capricious; Claims Court error reversed, protest denied

We conclude that it was not arbitrary and capricious for the Army Corps to determine that Anders's proposal lacked the required outline of administrative and recordkeeping procedures and that the Claims Court erred in its contrary determination.
11935: Bid protest relief: Claims Court improperly directed award to Anders where the Army Corps had made no fair and reasonable price determination; award directive vacated
It was error for the Claims Court to make a price-reasonability determination when the Army Corps had made no such determination.
12427: Bid protest merits: whether F3EA's proposal was unawardable for omitting teaming agreements. Court held the teaming agreement provisions were not material, so the protest fails on this ground.
We conclude that the Solicitation's teaming agreement provisions are not material requirements.
12428: Bid protest merits: whether the Army's investigation into the SSEB chairperson's alleged misconduct was adequate. Court held the investigation was not arbitrary and capricious.
nothing about the Army's investigation into the allegations relating to RM's role render the agency's decision to award the contract to F3EA arbitrary and capricious.
12429: Bid protest merits and prejudice: whether Lukos was financially responsible and thus ineligible for award, which bore on Oak Grove's prejudice. Court held the CFC's finding clearly erroneous and that the issue should have been remanded to the agency.
Accordingly, the Court of Federal Claims erred in finding that Lukos was ineligible to win the contract due to its lack of financial responsibility
13052: Bid protest merits: USPS's decision to split the 2022 solicitations into separate canine-screening and alarm-resolution solicitations was rational; MSA's challenge denied.
USPS's unbundling choice in 2022 readily passes muster under the applicable deferential standard of review.
13053: Bid protest merits: USPS's May 2022 shortening of the past-performance look-back period from 36 to 24 months was rational; MSA's challenge denied.
The May 2022 modification to the look-back period for examining past performance, shortening it from 36 to 24 months, is likewise rationally supported.
13054: Bid protest merits: Claims Court erred in holding USPS irrational in allowing MSA to bid in the 2022 solicitations despite its organizational conflict of interest; protests of AMK9 and GK9 denied and the injunction barring MSA reversed.

we agree with MSA that USPS had a rational basis for determining that MSA's former organizational conflict of interest had been mitigated sufficiently to warrant allowing MSA to bid in the 2022 Solicitations.
13625: Bid protest: whether the Navy's past performance rating and responsibility determination for Louis Berger, given the Spanish labor cases under DFARS 252.222-7002, were rational. Court found the decision rational on an alternative finding and did not decide the DFARS interpretation.
Based on these findings, we conclude that the Navy’s decision is supported by a rational basis.
13626: Bid protest: whether the Navy was rational in finding Louis Berger's staffing plan acceptable despite not staffing a Station Manager 24 hours a day under PWS 4.2. Protest denied.
Being able to contact a manager 24 hours a day does not necessarily mean that a manager must be staffed 24 hours a day.
14390: Bid protest merits: the agency's CICA stay override was arbitrary and capricious, so the protest was sustained; the protestor need not satisfy the four-factor preliminary injunction test to obtain declaratory relief.
A bid protestor seeking a declaration that an agency override of a CICA stay is arbitrary and capricious need only show that, in fact, the agency's override was arbitrary and capricious.
14750: Bid protest merits: whether the government acted with an improper motive in canceling the solicitation and whether it fairly considered Bear Mountainside's bid. The Court of Federal Claims denied the protest on judgment on the administrative record, and the Federal Circuit affirmed.
Relying largely on the Court of Federal Claims' thorough and detailed analysis of the facts and law, we affirm.
14926: Bid protest merits: whether F3EA's proposal was unawardable for failing to include teaming agreements; court held the teaming provisions were not material, so the protest was denied
We conclude that the Solicitation's teaming agreement provisions are not material requirements.
14927: Bid protest merits: whether the Army's investigation into the SSEB chairperson's alleged misconduct was adequate; court held it was not arbitrary and capricious and reversed the trial court's contrary finding
Thus, nothing about the Army's investigation into the allegations relating to RM's role render the agency's decision to award the contract to F3EA arbitrary and capricious.
14928: Bid protest prejudice: whether Lukos was financially responsible and thus ineligible for award; court held the trial court's finding clearly erroneous and that the question belonged to the agency, so Oak Grove could not show prejudice on the merits

The Court of Federal Claims erred in finding that Lukos was ineligible to win the contract due to its lack of financial responsibility and in concluding that Lukos' bid did not defeat Oak Grove's effort to satisfy the prejudice component of the merits of its claims.
15107: Bid protest merits: whether the agency's final corrective-action award was arbitrary, capricious, or unlawful, including whether the re-evaluation breached the presumption of good faith. Protest denied.
the agency's final award had a rational basis, and was not arbitrary, capricious, or an abuse of discretion.
